## Solution

$$I(a)=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{J_{1}(x)}{\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}}\,dx,\qquad a>0.$$

**Step 1. A Laplace representation of the kernel.**

The standard Laplace transform of $J_{0}$ (valid for $\operatorname{Re}a>0$) is
$$\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-at}J_{0}(xt)\,dt=\frac{1}{\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}}\,.$$
This follows from the series $J_{0}(xt)=\sum_{k\ge 0}(-1)^{k}\frac{(xt/2)^{2k}}{(k!)^{2}}$ and termwise integration, or equivalently from the integral representation $J_{0}(u)=\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}\cos(u\sin\theta)\,d\theta$ together with $\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-at}\cos(xt\sin\theta)\,dt=\frac{a}{a^{2}+x^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}$ and the evaluation $\frac{1}{\pi}\int_{0}^{\pi}\frac{a\,d\theta}{a^{2}+x^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}}$.

Hence
$$I(a)=\int_{0}^{\infty}J_{1}(x)\left(\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-at}J_{0}(xt)\,dt\right)dx.$$

**Step 2. Interchange the order of integration.**

The factor $e^{-at}$ makes the $t$‑integral absolutely convergent, and the inner $x$‑integral below is a classical Weber–Schafheitlin discontinuous integral (bounded in $t$). Interchanging (justified, e.g., by inserting a damping factor $e^{-\varepsilon x}$ and passing $\varepsilon\downarrow 0$, i.e. Abel summability) gives
$$I(a)=\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-at}\left(\int_{0}^{\infty}J_{1}(x)J_{0}(xt)\,dx\right)dt.$$

**Step 3. The Weber–Schafheitlin discontinuous integral.**

The classical formula (Watson, *Treatise on Bessel Functions*, §13.42; Gradshteyn–Ryzhik 6.574.2) states, for $\operatorname{Re}\nu>-1$,
$$\int_{0}^{\infty}J_{\nu+1}(Ax)\,J_{\nu}(Bx)\,dx=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{B^{\,\nu}}{A^{\nu+1}},&0<B<A,\\[6pt]
\dfrac{1}{2A},&B=A,\\[4pt]
0,&0<A<B.
\end{cases}$$

Take $\nu=0$, $A=1$, $B=t$:
$$\int_{0}^{\infty}J_{1}(x)J_{0}(tx)\,dx=
\begin{cases}
1,&0<t<1,\\
\tfrac12,&t=1,\\
0,&t>1.
\end{cases}$$

The single point $t=1$ is irrelevant to the outer integral, so the inner integral acts as the indicator $\mathbf{1}_{(0,1)}(t)$.

**Step 4. Evaluate the remaining integral.**

$$I(a)=\int_{0}^{1}e^{-at}\,dt=\left[-\frac{e^{-at}}{a}\right]_{0}^{1}=\frac{1-e^{-a}}{a}.$$

**Step 5. Consistency checks.**

- *Limit $a\to0^{+}$:* $\frac{1-e^{-a}}{a}\to1$. On the other side, $\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}\to x$, and $\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{J_{1}(x)}{x}\,dx=1$ (the classical Sonine value). ✓
- *Limit $a\to\infty$:* $\frac{1-e^{-a}}{a}\to0$, matching the fact that the kernel $\frac1{\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}}$ shrinks uniformly to $0$ on the effective support of $J_{1}$. ✓

---

$$\boxed{\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{J_{1}(x)}{\sqrt{a^{2}+x^{2}}}\,dx=\frac{1-e^{-a}}{a}},\qquad a>0.$$
